a1_answer:
NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION) — The proposed intervention is to introduce a corrosion-resistant nanocrystalline tin alloy coating on the lead positive grid surface that selectively forms a protective barrier against electrolyte penetration while maintaining electrical conductivity. Standard practice uses lead-antimony alloys (with antimony content typically 3-6%) to improve mechanical strength but increases corrosion rate; this mitigation replaces the corrosion-prone antimony with a nanocrystalline tin coating that forms a self-limiting oxide layer. The closest existing practice is tin alloying in lead grids (typically <2% tin for improved casting), but our intervention applies a pure tin coating as a surface barrier rather than alloying it throughout the grid structure, creating a more effective corrosion barrier without compromising bulk mechanical properties. The tin coating forms a stable SnO₂ layer that blocks oxygen diffusion to the lead substrate while maintaining electrical contact through the crystalline structure.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing relation is the parabolic oxidation law: x² = k·t, where x is oxide layer thickness, k is the corrosion rate constant, and t is time. The tin coating reduces k by forming a denser, more impervious oxide (SnO₂) with a diffusion coefficient for O²⁻ ions of ~10⁻¹⁷ cm²/s versus ~10⁻¹⁴ cm²/s for PbO. This reduces corrosion penetration by approximately 1000×. For a 15-year service life, the tin-coated grid would experience ~0.015 mm of corrosion penetration versus ~0.15 mm for standard lead-antimony, preserving grid cross-section integrity.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — Components: 1) Electroplating system with tin anodes, 2) Lead grid substrate with <2% antimony, 3) Surface preparation bath (alkaline cleaner, acid activator), 4) Electrolyte solution (stannous sulfate with fluoroboric acid additive), 5) Rinse system, 6) Drying oven. Materials: High-purity tin (99.99%) for anodes, fluoroboric acid (HBF₄), stannous sulfate (SnSO₄), lead-antimony alloy grid (antimony ≤2%). Procedure: 1) Clean grids in alkaline bath (60°C, 5 min), 2) Activate in 5% sulfuric acid (2 min), 3) Electroplate at 20 mA/cm² for 2 min to achieve 2-3 μm coating, 4) Rinse in deionized water, 5) Dry at 80°C for 30 min. Development needed: Optimization of plating parameters for uniform coating on complex grid geometries.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — Installability: Similar to current grid manufacturing with additional plating line (medium burden). Operability: No change to battery operation (same burden). Maintenance: No additional maintenance required (same burden). Cost: ~15% higher grid manufacturing cost offset by longer service life (net neutral). The plating process requires additional equipment but uses standard electroplating techniques familiar to battery manufacturers. The coating thickness control requires process monitoring but within standard quality control capabilities for battery manufacturing.

EXECUTIBLE TEST — Protocol: Build two identical battery banks (20 cells each), one with standard lead-antimony grids (antimony ~4%) and one with tin-coated grids (antimony ≤2%). Subject both to 2.27 V/cell float charge at 40°C with weekly capacity measurements. Instruments: Automated capacity testing system, internal resistance measurement, grid cross-section analysis at end of test. Pass/fail threshold: Tin-coated batteries must maintain ≥90% initial capacity after 15 years (accelerated equivalent) while standard batteries fall below 80%. Duration: 6 months at 40°C (equivalent to ~15 years at 25°C). Kill criterion: If tin-coated batteries show >10% higher degradation rate than standard batteries at any point, the intervention is falsified.
